newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Lower S.Africa imports a sign of cooling economy.
newsitem.headline: Lower S.Africa imports a sign of cooling economy.

text.p: A sharp slowdown in South Africa's imports in May was a further sign of a cooling economy already evidenced by recent GDP data, E.W. Balderson economist Mike Schussler said on Thursday.
Imports rose just 8.7 percent year-on-year in May compared with export growth of 38.6 percent.
The result was a trade surplus of 1.746 billion rand in the month -- double economists' forecasts and up from 730 million rand in April.
E.W. Balderson economist Mike Schussler said that at 8.7 percent, imports were rising at a slower pace than inflation, currently 9.5 percent.
"In real terms, imports are actually negative at the moment and if it wasn't for the mineral category it would have been even more," Schussler said.
The minerals category mainly consists of South African oil imports and are volatile on a month-to-month basis.
"The slowdown in imports probably reflects a slowdown in the economy in consumer spending, probably capital spending and overall GDP," Schussler said.
Gross Domestic Product declined by 0.8 percent in the first quarter of 1997.
Standard Bank Economics Division noted that exports had primarily been driven higher by a 40 percent and 57 percent month-on-month rise in chemical and vehicle exports respectively.
Vegetable exports, which have risen sharply over the last four months, rose by 190 percent year-on-year, Schussler said.
Standard Bank said the rise in exports continued to reveal the positive impact of a depreciated rand and that the trend remained "strongly upwards".
